9503.etyen:
Inherited from Danish deig, older spelling of dej, from Old Norse deig, from Proto-Germanic *daigaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to knead, form”). Compare Icelandic deig, Faroese deiggj, Swedish deg, English dough, Dutch deeg, German Teig.
Further notes
Mid-19th-century Danish retained an otherwise archaic spelling with ⟨ig⟩ or ⟨ug⟩ in a small number of words, namely boug, deig, feig, laug, ploug, saug, seig, toug. All of these have since been regularized to bov, dej, fej, lav, plov, sav, sej, tov. In Norway, however, the older spellings were retained as they fit in with native dialect

1001503.etyen:
The modern given name has more than one possible origin. In Norwegian, Nanna has been used as a nursery-language pet form of female given names such as Andrea. It has also been analysed as a pet form of Anna, Johanna, Amanda and Marianne.
Under the Anna analysis, the name ultimately belongs to the same name family as Late Latin Anna, from Koine Greek Ἄννα (Ánna, “Anna”), from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (Ḥannāh, “Hannah; grace, favour”).
Modern Norwegian use was additionally reinforced by the Nordic name revival through the Old Norse mythological name Nanna, discussed under Etymology 2.
